newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurotunnel seeks new lifeline with debt deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurotunnel seeks new lifeline with debt deal.

text.p: Eurotunnel Plc said on Thursday it had clinched an agreement with its lead banks to restructure nearly nine billion pounds ($14.6 billion) of debt -- the first major hurdle to making it financially secure for the next six years.

But the Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel warned that it needs an extension on its 65-year tunnel operating concession if it is to win approval for the restructuring from all of its 225 lending banks as well as its shareholders.
"The extension of the concession is essential to securing the banks' and shareholders' approval," co-chairman Patrick Ponsolle told reporters at a news conference.

Ponsolle said the group was pushing for a concession of as long as 999 years. Its current concession is due to expire in 2052, leaving the group with little scope to make a return for investors and banks.
So far such moves have been resisted and seen as a back-door subsidy, according to analysts.

But while Eurotunnel has put in a claim for a thousand-year lease Ponsolle made clear it was open to negotiation with the two governments, noting that the last extension granted was for 10 years, "and that was considered significant."

Managing director George Chazot later told Reuters it remained to be seen what term might prove acceptable to the governments on one side and the shareholders and banks on the other. "We are in the middle," he said.

But he acknowledged that 99 years might be more realistic. "Certainly 99 years would be substantial. It is essential to getting approval for the debt deal from shareholders and the (remaining) banks," said Chazot.

If shareholders and the 225-strong banking syndicate approved the deal this year, Eurotunnel would be free to concentrate on improving its operating performance, it said. The company said it aimed to make an operating profit in 1997 for the first time in its history.

But Richard Hannah, analyst at UBS and a seller of the shares, told Reuters "What they are saying is 'We can break even if we ignore our nine billion in debt.' It's like someone saying 'I'm doing well as long as I ignore my overdraft.' They are going to have to do a lot better to make this work."
Eurotunnel, struggling with heavy debts due to cost overruns in building the tunnel, suffered more problems last November when a fire cut its traffic sharply.

The substance of the debt deal is unchanged from termsoutlined last October. Shareholders will have the chance to keep the right to 54.5 percent of long-term potential profits but would have to subscribe for more shares which are due to be swapped under the deal for some of the debt.

Ponsolle and his British co-chairman Robert Malpas said in a statement that Eurotunnel's steering committee of bankers had approved the final debt deal. But now details would be presented in a prospectus to be issued to shareholders and all the banks in mid-May.
Eurotunnel was upbeat about its longer-term potential, telling investors in a statement it expected "to increase our market share...one can hardly say it has peaked".

The debt news pushed Eurotunnel shares in London and Paris higher even though it reported a 1996 loss of 685 million pounds ($1.1 billion), compared with a 1995 loss of 924 million pounds, after interest charges.

The loss was in line with expectations so markets focused on the debt development which they saw as positive. The shares rose 4-I/2 pence in London to 74 pence and three percent to 6.7 francs in Paris.
Shares in rival P&O, which operates cross-Channel ferries, slid 11 1/2 pence to 600 on the news that Eurotunnel could be heading towards a firmer financial footing to fight for market share.
Eurotunnel's 1996 turnover rose to 448 million pounds from 282 million the year before.
Eurotunnel said the first quarter of 1997 went well, with traffic reaching "very satisfactory levels" and fares stabilising after a price-war with the ferry companies.
Ponsolle and Malpas said "1996 was a good year for the group" despite the fire.
The blaze on November 18, 1996 hit tourist traffic and halted freight traffic, although it is due to resume in mid-June after repairs to the tunnel.

They were confident that the Le Shuttle train service would regain the 50 percent market share lost due to the fire by the end of 1997. So far, it had recovered 80 percent of the market share achieved before the fire.
Traffic on the Eurostar passenger train service, owned by London and Continental Railways, also rose 25 percent in the first quarter of 1997 from the same time in 1996.

A meeting of shareholders has been set for June 24 to approve the debt restructuring deal but Ponsolle said it was likely to be delayed to July 10 to attract the 25 percent quorum of shareholders required under French law.

"The main merit (of the debt plan) is to ensure the financial stability of the group for the six years to come, allowing the management to focus principally on the improvement of the group's performance," said the chairmen.

They said in a letter to investors that shareholders "have been disappointed by the financial performance of the group so far and by the need to envisage a financial restructuring that will dilute their position".
But they added that this deal was "the best possible compromise under the present circumstances".
($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
